subject: operating-systems
title: Threads and process resources
summary: Threads are schedulable execution flows that share a process address space and many process-owned resources.

questions.prompt: Which resource is normally private to each thread in a multithreaded process?
questions.answerKey: Each thread has its own stack for call frames and local execution state.
questions.explanation: Threads commonly share code, heap, and process-level file descriptors.

questions.prompt: What is a major benefit of using multiple threads in one process?
options: They can share an address space with lower communication overhead
They guarantee parallel execution on one core
They give each thread a separate process address space
questions.answerKey: Threads can communicate through shared memory without separate process address spaces.
questions.explanation: Synchronization is still required, and one core cannot execute two instructions simultaneously.

questions.prompt: A thread waits for a condition variable while another thread updates shared data. What should the waiting thread do?
options: Wait and recheck the predicate after notification
questions.answerKey: Condition waits should be enclosed in a loop that rechecks the protected predicate.
questions.explanation: Spurious wakeups and races between notification and reacquisition make a loop necessary.

questions.prompt: If one thread performs an invalid memory access in a typical user process, what is the likely scope of failure?
options: Only that thread is always killed and the process continues
The process may be terminated because threads share the address space
Only the kernel thread is affected
No thread can observe the fault
questions.answerKey: A fatal memory fault generally compromises the shared process and may terminate it.
questions.explanation: The exact signal and recovery policy are OS-specific, but threads do not provide address-space isolation.

questions.prompt: Compare a process and a thread in terms of address space and scheduling.
questions.answerKey: A process provides an isolated address space and owns resources; threads are execution paths within a process, share most of its address space and resources, and are scheduled as runnable units by the OS or runtime.
questions.explanation: Do not claim that every thread has a separate process address space.

questions.prompt: Give two pieces of state a context switch between threads must preserve and explain why.
questions.answerKey: Examples include the program counter/instruction pointer, stack pointer, general registers, and scheduling state. They must be saved so the switched-out thread can resume at the same instruction with its call stack and computation intact.
questions.explanation: Kernel details differ, but execution registers and stack context are essential.
